Index notation

Words: 40
Multilinear algebra OurBigBook.com
Index notation describes vectors, matrices and tensors by their components relative to a chosen basis. For example, matrix multiplication reads (AB)ij​=∑k​Aik​Bkj​. The free indices i,j identify the resulting component, while k is summed. An explicit summation sign avoids depending on an implicit Einstein summation convention.

Coalgebra ((C,Δ,ε))

Words: 355 Articles: 12
Multilinear algebra OurBigBook.com
A comonoid in the monoidal category of modules over a commutative ring, with tensor ⊗k​ and unit k.

Coideal (ΔI⊆I⊗C+C⊗I,ε(I)=0)

Words: 36
Coalgebra OurBigBook.com
A linear subspace I of a coalgebra satisfying the displayed conditions. These are exactly the conditions for the comultiplication and counit to descend to the quotient vector space C/I. An ideal that is also a coideal in a bialgebra gives a quotient bialgebra.

Measuring coalgebra (p(c)(ab)=∑p(c(1)​)(a)p(c(2)​)(b))

Words: 63 Articles: 1
Coalgebra OurBigBook.com
For unital algebras over a field A,B, a coalgebra C measures A into B when a linear map p:C→Homk​(A,B) satisfies the displayed identity and p(c)(1A​)=ε(c)1B​. Group-like elements therefore act by unital algebra homomorphisms over a field.

Universal measuring coalgebra (P(A,B))

Words: 36
Measuring coalgebra OurBigBook.com
A terminal measuring coalgebra: every measuring map from C factors uniquely through its universal measuring map by a coalgebra homomorphism C→P(A,B). Composition of universal measurings makes P(A,A) a bialgebra, with the identity map providing its unit.

Group-like element (Δg=g⊗g,ε(g)=1)

Words: 17
Coalgebra OurBigBook.com
An element of a coalgebra satisfying the displayed identities. A group-like element in a Hopf algebra is invertible with inverse its antipode image.

Comodule ((M,ρ))

Words: 170 Articles: 5
Coalgebra OurBigBook.com
A right comodule is an object M with a coaction ρ:M→M⊗C satisfying the coassociativity and counit laws. This definition extends from coalgebras to comonoids in a monoidal category.

Words: 60 Articles: 1
Comodule OurBigBook.com
A natural underlying transformation of tensor bifunctors on right comodules over a field has components φM,N​(u⊗v)=∑u(0)​⊗v(0)​γ(u(1)​,v(1)​). Recover γ=(ε⊗ε)φH,H​; colinearity and monoidal axioms impose further equations.
Multiplication compatibility for a comodule tensor transformation (m∗γ=γ∗n)
Words: 32
Comodule tensor transformation formula OurBigBook.com
For a transformation from the tensor built using n to the tensor built using m, colinearity is m∗γ=γ∗n: ∑m(a(1)​,b(1)​)γ(a(2)​,b(2)​)=∑γ(a(1)​,b(1)​)n(a(2)​,b(2)​). Scalar maps enter this convolution product for coalgebra maps via the common algebra unit.

Corestriction functor for comodules (f∗​)

Words: 64 Articles: 1
Comodule OurBigBook.com
A comonoid morphism f:H→K induces a functor f∗​ on right comodules, replacing ρ by (1⊗f)ρ and preserving underlying objects and arrows. For bimonoids, it is strict monoidal exactly when f is also a monoid morphism.
Comodule natural transformation formula (βM​(u)=∑u(0)​α(u(1)​))
Words: 31
Corestriction functor for comodules OurBigBook.com
A natural transformation between corestriction functors over a field has components βM​(u)=∑u(0)​α(u(1)​), recovered by α=εβH​. Monoidality forces α to be a unital algebra homomorphism over a field; for a Hopf algebra, αS supplies the inverse.

Coaction (ρ:M→M⊗C)

Words: 21
Comodule OurBigBook.com
The structure map of a comodule; a right coaction satisfies (ρ⊗1)ρ=(1⊗Δ)ρ with coherent parentheses, and (1⊗ε)ρ is the inverse right unitor.

Convolution product for coalgebra maps (f∗g=mA​(f⊗g)ΔC​)

Words: 30
Coalgebra OurBigBook.com
For a coalgebra C and a unital associative algebra over a commutative ring A, maps f,g:C→A have convolution f∗g=mA​(f⊗g)ΔC​, with unit jA​εC​. The two-sided convolution inverse of 1H​ is the antipode.

Sweedler notation (Δh=∑h(1)​⊗h(2)​)

Words: 25
Coalgebra OurBigBook.com
The notation Δh=∑h(1)​⊗h(2)​ suppresses the summation index of a comultiplication; iterated indices use coassociativity. For a comodule, write ρ(u)=∑u(0)​⊗u(1)​.

Multilinear map

Words: 447 Articles: 6
Multilinear algebra OurBigBook.com
A multilinear map F:V1​×⋯×Vr​→W is a map between vector spaces that is linear in each argument when all other arguments are fixed. For example the evaluation (ω,v)↦ω(v) is bilinear, and the determinant is multilinear in its columns. The universal property of a tensor product replaces this separate linearity by a single linear map from V1​⊗⋯⊗Vr​.

Bilinear map

Words: 401 Articles: 5
Multilinear map OurBigBook.com
A bilinear map is a map B:V×W→U between vector spaces that is linear in each argument when the other is fixed. The nonlinear temperature advection can be written as the diagonal of a bilinear map, N(ϕ,χ)=−u[ϕ]⋅∇χ, when velocity depends linearly on temperature. Unlike a bilinear form, its output need not be a scalar.

Bilinearity

Words: 52
Bilinear map OurBigBook.com
A map B:V×W→Z between vector spaces is bilinear when it is linear in either argument with the other held fixed. A scalar-valued bilinear form is the case V=W and Z is the scalar field. Checking bilinearity is one of the algebraic steps in verifying a real inner product; being a symmetric bilinear form and having positive squared norm impose further conditions.

Symmetric bilinear diagonal-parallel lemma (S(u,v)=V(u)v+V(v)u)

Words: 81
Bilinear map OurBigBook.com
Let S:W×W→W be a symmetric bilinear map on a finite-dimensional real vector space. If S(v,v) is parallel to v for every v, then it has the displayed form for one covector V. Write S(ei​,ei​)=αi​ei​ in a basis. Applying the condition to ei​+ej​ and ei​−ej​ excludes every component outside their span and gives S(ei​,ej​)=(αj​ei​+αi​ej​)/2. Set V(ei​)=αi​/2 and extend by bilinearity. Dimension one follows by the same definition. The trace identity Saac​=(n+1)Vc​ proves uniqueness without depending on the chosen basis.

Derivative of a continuous bilinear map (Df(a,b)(h,k)=f(h,b)+f(a,k))

Words: 38
Bilinear map OurBigBook.com
A continuous bilinear map obeys ∥f(h,k)∥≤C∥h∥∥k∥. Expanding f(a+h,b+k) leaves the displayed linear term and remainder f(h,k). For product norm ρ=(∥h∥2+∥k∥2)1/2, the remainder has norm at most Cρ2/2, hence is o(ρ). This proves the Fréchet derivative formula.

Rank bound for a nonsingular complex bilinear map (rankϕ≥dimU+dimV−1)

Words: 92
Bilinear map OurBigBook.com
Let U,V be nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, and let ϕ:U⊗V→W have injective restrictions when either nonzero factor is fixed. It induces a map from CPa−1×CPb−1 to CPr−1, where a=dimU, b=dimV, and r=rankϕ. Pullback of the degree-two generator is x+y, since both factor restrictions are projective linear embeddings. Its (a+b−2)th power is (a−1a+b−2​)xa−1yb−1=0 in integral cohomology. The target must therefore have complex dimension at least a+b−2. Positivity of both factor dimensions is necessary; a zero factor can make the claimed inequality false.

Complex bilinear dimension bound (dimimϕ≥dimU+dimV−1)

Words: 87
Bilinear map OurBigBook.com
For nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector spaces U,V, suppose a bilinear map never vanishes on a pair of nonzero vectors. Equivalently, each map obtained by fixing one nonzero argument is injective. If its associated map on U⊗V has image dimension r, projectivization gives a map to CPr−1 whose positive degree-two class pulls back to x+y. The nonzero top power (x+y)dimU+dimV−2 in the product cohomology ring of complex projective space proves the bound. Multiplication of polynomials of bounded degree attains equality. Nonzero hypotheses matter: with a zero factor, slice conditions can be vacuous.

Alternating multilinear map

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Multilinear algebra OurBigBook.com
An alternating multilinear map vanishes whenever two arguments are equal. Swapping two arguments reverses its sign.

Alternating trilinear form

Words: 49
Alternating multilinear map OurBigBook.com
An alternating trilinear form is a scalar-valued map, linear in three arguments, which vanishes whenever two arguments agree. In characteristic zero, interchanging two arguments negates its value, while cyclic permutation preserves it. For a symmetric bilinear form B on a Lie algebra, the tensor B([x,y],z) is alternating exactly when B is an invariant bilinear form on a Lie algebra.

Tensor product (⊗)

Words: 2k Articles: 19
Multilinear algebra OurBigBook.com
A tensor product turns a bilinear map into a linear map. For vector spaces V,W over the same field F, its elements are finite sums of pure tensors v⊗w, subject to bilinearity:
(v+v′)⊗wv⊗(w+w′)(av)⊗w​=v⊗w+v′⊗w,=v⊗w+v⊗w′,=a(v⊗w)=v⊗(aw).​
(1)
The scalar a belongs to F; writing V⊗F​W makes this choice explicit. These rules preserve separate linearity while allowing arbitrary linear combinations of products.[ref]
For a concrete example, take V=W=R2, with basis vectors e1​,e2​ in the first copy and f1​,f2​ in the second. The four tensor-product basis elements are
e1​⊗f1​,e1​⊗f2​,e2​⊗f1​,e2​⊗f2​.
(2)
The pure tensor made from v=2e1​+e2​ and w=−f1​+3f2​ expands to
v⊗w=−2e1​⊗f1​+6e1​⊗f2​−e2​⊗f1​+3e2​⊗f2​.
(3)
Each basis vector in one factor can interact with each basis vector in the other. This is why dimensions multiply; the tensor-product coefficient matrix displays these four interactions as a two-by-two grid.
The tensor product is different from the Cartesian product V×W. With componentwise vector addition and scalar multiplication, the latter contains pairs and has dimension dimV+dimW. The map τ(v,w)=v⊗w is bilinear, generally neither linear on that Cartesian product nor injective nor surjective. In our example, τ(2v,2w)=4τ(v,w), and τ(2v,w/2)=τ(v,w); the separability of a tensor explains why some outputs cannot be reached at all. Both spaces happen to have dimension four when V=W=R2, but this coincidence does not identify their structures.

Universal property of a tensor product (B=L∘τ)

Words: 196
Tensor product OurBigBook.com
For a bilinear map B:V×W→U, there is exactly one linear map L:V⊗F​W→U satisfying L(v⊗w)=B(v,w). Equivalently, B=L∘τ, where τ(v,w)=v⊗w. The universal property of a tensor product concerns the vector space together with this distinguished bilinear map.[ref]
Here is a complete calculation over the real numbers. Define the bilinear map
B(v,w)=(v1​w1​+2v1​w2​+v2​w2​, v2​w1​−v1​w2​).
(4)
Its values on pairs of basis vectors determine L on the four tensor-product basis elements:
L(e1​⊗f1​)L(e2​⊗f1​)​=(1,0),=(0,1),​L(e1​⊗f2​)L(e2​⊗f2​)​=(2,−1),=(1,0).​
(5)
Consequently, for t=∑i,j=12​cij​ei​⊗fj​,
L(t)=(c11​+2c12​+c22​, c21​−c12​).
(6)
For v=(2,1) and w=(−1,3), the direct calculation gives B(v,w)=(−2+12+3,−1−6)=(13,−7). Using the expansion of v⊗w instead gives L(v⊗w)=−2(1,0)+6(2,−1)−(0,1)+3(1,0)=(13,−7). The linear map also handles a nonseparable tensor such as t=e1​⊗f1​+e2​⊗f2​: L(t)=(2,0), even though no single pair has v⊗w=t.
A short proof uses a tensor-product basis: assign L(ei​⊗fj​)=B(ei​,fj​) and extend by linearity. Expanding both inputs verifies L(v⊗w)=B(v,w) by bilinearity; the assigned values on a basis force uniqueness. More generally, every multilinear map F:V1​×⋯×Vr​→U factors uniquely through a linear map from V1​⊗⋯⊗Vr​. This lets formulas involving several inputs define linear maps without choosing coordinates; tensor contraction uses the evaluation pairing between a vector and a covector.

Tensor-product basis ({ei​⊗fj​},dim(V⊗F​W)=dimVdimW)

Words: 225 Articles: 1
Tensor product OurBigBook.com
If (e1​,…,em​) and (f1​,…,fn​) are bases of finite-dimensional vector spaces V,W over F, then the mn products ei​⊗fj​ form a basis of V⊗F​W. There is one independent coordinate for every pair of indices.[ref]
For a proof outline, bilinearity expands each pure tensor as
(∑i​vi​ei​)⊗(∑j​wj​fj​)=∑i,j​vi​wj​(ei​⊗fj​),
(7)
so these products form a spanning set. For linear independence, take the coordinate functionals ek,fℓ from the two dual bases. The bilinear map (v,w)↦ek(v)fℓ(w) induces a linear functional λkℓ​ on the tensor product, satisfying λkℓ​(ei​⊗fj​)=δki​δℓj​. Applying it to a proposed zero linear combination selects just ckℓ​, forcing every coefficient to vanish. Thus dimensions multiply, rather than add. This finite-dimensional count includes a zero factor, whose tensor product has dimension zero.

Tensor-product coefficient matrix (C(t)=(cij​))

Words: 112
Tensor-product basis OurBigBook.com
After choosing ordered bases, identify a tensor t=∑i,j​cij​ei​⊗fj​ with its matrix C(t)=(cij​). This is a linear isomorphism between V⊗F​W and the vector space of m-by-n matrices: each tensor-product basis element becomes the matrix with one entry equal to one and all others zero. In particular, a pure tensor has the outer product coefficient formula
C(v⊗w)=vwT,C((2,1)⊗(−1,3))=(−2−1​63​).
(8)
Here v,w on the right denote column coordinate vectors. The identification depends on the chosen bases, while the tensor itself does not. Over the complex numbers, the same formula uses the ordinary transpose wT, with no complex conjugation; replacing it by the conjugate transpose w∗ would conjugate the scalar in the second input, violating bilinearity.

Separability of a tensor (t=v⊗w)

Words: 194
Tensor product OurBigBook.com
In a two-factor tensor product over a field, a pure tensor is also called a separable or decomposable tensor: it can be expressed as one product v⊗w. Every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors, but a sum need not itself be a pure tensor.[ref]
For finite-dimensional vector spaces, the tensor-product coefficient matrix gives a decisive test: a nonzero tensor is a pure tensor exactly when its matrix rank is one. Indeed, every column of vwT is a scalar multiple of v. Conversely, if all columns of a nonzero matrix are multiples of one nonzero column v, collect their multipliers in w to obtain C=vwT. The zero tensor is also a pure tensor, for example 0⊗w, but its matrix rank is zero.
In R2⊗R​R2, the tensor
t=e1​⊗f1​+e2​⊗f2​,C(t)=(10​01​),
(9)
is nonseparable: its matrix rank is two and its determinant is one, whereas det(vwT)=0. Directly, trying t=(ae1​+be2​)⊗(cf1​+df2​) requires ac=bd=1 and ad=bc=0. The first two equations force all four scalars nonzero, contradicting the others. In contrast, products sharing a factor do combine: e1​⊗f1​+e1​⊗f2​=e1​⊗(f1​+f2​). Thus being written as two summands alone does not establish nonseparability.

Two-factor tensor rank (rank⊗​(t)=rankC(t))

Words: 144
Tensor product OurBigBook.com
The two-factor tensor rank is the smallest number of pure tensors whose sum equals t, with zero allowed as the empty sum. For two finite-dimensional vector spaces over the same field, it equals the matrix rank of the tensor-product coefficient matrix. A sum of r outer products has column space contained in the span of their r first factors, so its matrix rank is at most r. Conversely, choose a basis u1​,…,ur​ for the column space, express each column in that basis, and collect the coefficients into row vectors wkT​. This yields C=∑k=1r​uk​wkT​, hence a sum of r pure tensors.
The pure tensor (2,1)⊗(−1,3) therefore has two-factor tensor rank one, whereas e1​⊗f1​+e2​⊗f2​ has two-factor tensor rank two. Both have two factors: the number of factors and the minimum number of product summands are different counts. Over the real numbers, the singular value decomposition supplies a useful decomposition C=∑k​σk​uk​vkT​, with one nonzero term per matrix rank. The two-factor rank equality does not extend to three or more factors by merely choosing one matrix layout.

Tensor algebra (T(V))

Words: 611 Articles: 13
Tensor product OurBigBook.com
The tensor algebra of a vector space V is the graded algebra
T(V)=⨁n≥0​V⊗n,
(10)
with multiplication given by concatenation of tensors.

Truncated tensor algebra (T(N)(V)=⨁k=0N​V⊗k)

Words: 42
Tensor algebra OurBigBook.com
The truncated tensor algebra discards products of degree greater than N. Its multiplication is (a⊗b)(k)=∑j=0k​a(j)⊗b(k−j). Every element with scalar part 1 is invertible by a finite geometric series in its positive-degree part. Truncated exponential and logarithm are finite polynomials.

Tensor power (V⊗n)

Words: 36 Articles: 1
Tensor algebra OurBigBook.com
The nth tensor power is the iterated tensor product of modules V⊗n=V⊗⋯⊗V.
Tensor square (V⊗V)
Words: 25
Tensor power OurBigBook.com
The tensor square is the second tensor power V⊗2=V⊗V. Over a field of characteristic different from two it decomposes as the direct sum of the symmetric square and exterior square.

Symmetric algebra (S(V))

Words: 516 Articles: 9
Tensor algebra OurBigBook.com
The symmetric algebra is the quotient of T(V) by the ideal generated by v⊗w−w⊗v. It is graded by symmetric powers:
S(V)=⨁n≥0​SnV.
(11)
Symmetric power (SnV)
Words: 493 Articles: 8
Symmetric algebra OurBigBook.com
The nth symmetric power SnV is the quotient of V⊗n that identifies tensors differing by a permutation of their factors. Equivalently, over characteristic zero it is the subspace of symmetric tensors.
Weight-transfer proof of irreducibility of symmetric powers (Eij​⋅xa=aj​xa+ei​−ej​)
Words: 93
Symmetric power OurBigBook.com
In the symmetric power SymmCn of the defining unitary group representation, diagonal torus weights are indexed by nonnegative integer tuples summing to m, with one monomial per weight space. Torus averaging extracts a monomial from any nonzero invariant complex subspace. The complexified Lie algebra acts by Eij​=xi​∂xj​​ on the symmetric algebra. Whenever aj​>0, the displayed action moves one unit of degree from j to i with nonzero coefficient. Finite transfers connect every degree-m monomial, so the subspace is the entire representation. The case m=0 is the one-dimensional trivial representation. This proof needs neither the Weyl character formula nor the Weyl dimension formula.

Exterior algebra (Λ∙V)

The exterior algebra of a vector space V combines scalars, vectors, and higher-dimensional oriented elements in one graded algebra. In a finite-dimensional vector space it is

(13)
with multiplication given by the exterior product. Degree zero is the scalar field, degree one is V, and degree two is the space of bivectors. Multiplication adds degrees: combining two vectors produces a bivector, rather than another ordinary vector.[ref]
The essential rule is v∧v=0. Repeating the same direction cannot produce a nonzero oriented area. Bilinearity then gives u∧v=−v∧u: expand (u+v)∧(u+v)=0 and remove the two zero self-products. The alternating rule remains part of the definition in characteristic two, where sign reversal alone would not force a self-product to vanish.
If V=R2 with standard basis e1​,e2​, every element of its exterior algebra has the form
a+be1​+ce2​+d(e1​∧e2​).
(14)
There are four independent coefficients: one scalar, two vector components, and one area component. In R3, the respective degree dimensions are 1,3,3,1, giving eight components in total. More generally, the exterior power basis gives total dimension ∑k=0n​(kn​)=2n.
This language is useful when direction and orientation matter together. Determinants measure the action on top-degree exterior powers; differential forms use exterior powers of a dual space to describe quantities integrated along paths, surfaces, and higher-dimensional regions. The Grassmann algebra viewpoint also makes the sign changes in anticommuting generators systematic. A single multiplication rule connects geometry and algebra.

Determinant (det)

Multilinear algebra OurBigBook.com
The determinant assigns a scalar to a square matrix. For a linear map on the real plane, it measures signed area scaling: its absolute value tells how much area grows, and its sign records whether the orientation of a vector space is preserved or reversed. In three dimensions, the same idea measures signed volume. Over a field, a square matrix is an invertible matrix exactly when its determinant is nonzero. These are two views of one phenomenon: losing an independent direction collapses full-dimensional volume and makes the original input impossible to recover uniquely.[ref]
Start with an explicit matrix and its action on a vector:
A=(21​13​),A(xy​)=(2x+yx+3y​),det(ac​bd​)=ad−bc,detA=2⋅3−1⋅1=5.​
(38)
The columns are the images of the standard basis vectors: Ae1​=(2,1)T and Ae2​=(1,3)T. Consequently the unit square with corners (0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1) becomes the parallelogram with corners (0,0),(2,1),(3,4),(1,3). Its area is five. Every small patch of this square undergoes the same linear map, so the factor describes the whole deformation, rather than just one specially chosen boundary. The matrix mixes horizontal and vertical components, but its determinant compresses that combined effect into one area factor.[ref]
Now exchange the columns:
Aswap​=(13​21​),detAswap​=1⋅1−2⋅3=−5.
(39)
The parallelogram occupies exactly the same region, but its generating vectors arrive in the opposite order. Moving from the first column to the second now turns clockwise rather than counterclockwise. Ordinary area remains five; the oriented volume in two dimensions changes sign. A negative determinant therefore signals reversed orientation of a vector space, not a negative amount of material. Keeping the sign makes successive reversals calculable: two reversals restore the original orientation of a vector space.
Compare a singular matrix:
C=(12​24​),detC=1⋅4−2⋅2=0,C(xy​)=(x+2y)(12​).
(40)
Its columns are linearly dependent: the second is twice the first. The unit square collapses onto the segment from (0,0) to (3,6), which has zero area despite nonzero length. Since C(−2,1)T=0, the kernel of a linear map contains a nonzero vector; inputs differing by that vector have identical outputs. The collapsed picture explains why an inverse matrix cannot exist.
For A, recovery is possible, and the complete matrix multiplication check is
A−1=51​(3−1​−12​),AA−1=51​(2⋅3+1(−1)1⋅3+3(−1)​2(−1)+1⋅21(−1)+3⋅2​)=(10​01​)=I.
(41)
Here I is the identity matrix. The inverse matrix restores the original square, shrinking its area by 1/5. Generally, the adjugate identity gives A−1=adj(A)/detA whenever the determinant is nonzero over a field; this is why the denominator matters.[ref]
The multiplicativity of the determinant describes two successive deformations. Matrix multiplication means that AB applies B first, then A. Take
B=(10​02​),AB=(2⋅1+1⋅01⋅1+3⋅0​2⋅0+1⋅21⋅0+3⋅2​)=(21​26​).
(42)
The first linear map doubles area; the second multiplies the resulting area by five. Thus the unit square passes through areas 1,2,10, with the last parallelogram bounded by (0,0),(2,1),(4,7),(2,6). Direct calculation agrees:
detB=2,det(AB)=2⋅6−2⋅1=10=detAdetB.
(43)
This explains physically why area factors multiply instead of adding. The general identity holds for square matrices of the same size, including singular matrices. If either stage loses a direction, later processing cannot recover the discarded information.[ref]
The same interpretation works in three dimensions without drawing a new picture. The diagonal matrix
D=​200​030​00−1​​,detD=2⋅3⋅(−1)=−6
(44)
sends the unit cube to a rectangular box with side lengths two, three, and one. Its ordinary volume is six. The minus sign comes from reversing the third direction, so the oriented volume is minus six. Replacing the last diagonal entry by zero flattens the cube into a planar region: its area may be positive, but its three-dimensional volume is zero. This distinction matters whenever a linear map changes shape: the determinant measures size in the full input dimension, rather than the size of whichever lower-dimensional object remains.
The determinant measures neither trace nor perimeter. For A, the trace happens also to be five, but the identity matrix in two dimensions has trace two and determinant one. The first parallelogram above has perimeter 2(5​+10​), compared with four for the unit square; boundary length follows a different rule. Nor does determinant one require every length to stay fixed: the diagonal matrix diag(2,1/2) preserves area while stretching one direction and compressing the other.
These properties make the determinant useful when coordinates obscure what a deformation does. A nonzero determinant certifies that linearly independent input directions remain distinguishable; its magnitude counts the area or volume represented by a transformed cell. That second role reappears in the change of variables formula, where the Jacobian determinant corrects the sizes of small cells. Signed volume also separates a deformation that reverses the orientation of a vector space from one that merely stretches it, even when both give identical ordinary volume factors.[ref]
For general n, regard the columns v1​,…,vn​ as ordered arguments. The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear map to the scalar field normalized by detI=1. The multilinearity of the determinant means linearity in each column separately, with all others held fixed:
det(…,αu+βv,…)=αdet(…,u,…)+βdet(…,v,…).
(45)
Alternation means equal columns give zero; exchanging columns negates the result. Normalization sets the oriented volume of the standard basis to one. These properties also hold in rows. For real three-dimensional columns, their determinant is the scalar triple product, and its absolute value is the enclosed volume. Over other fields, the algebraic definition still works even without a geometric notion of positive volume.[ref]
Separate linearity does not mean the determinant is a linear map on the whole matrix. Scaling every column of an n-by-n matrix by t gives det(tA)=tndetA. For our two-dimensional example, det(2A)=4detA=20: doubling both directions quadruples area. The power records how many independent directions are being scaled together.
The properties suggest practical computations. Adding a multiple of one column to another preserves the determinant: the extra term has repeated columns and vanishes. This is the algebra behind an area-preserving shear mapping. Alternatively, expansion along a row uses cofactors, each a matrix minor multiplied by a sign:
detA=∑j=1n​aij​(−1)i+jdetA(ij),
(46)
where A(ij) deletes row i and column j. The Leibniz formula for determinants supplies the general entry formula. Both calculations encode the same geometric invariant; the defining properties explain their structure without requiring memorization of a separate recipe for every size.[ref]

The row formula follows from the Leibniz formula for determinants by grouping permutations according to the selected column in row i. For a lower triangular matrix, expanding along the first row reduces the determinant to A11​ times a smaller triangular determinant; induction gives the product of all diagonal entries, even when some vanish.

Nonintersecting lattice-path determinant

Words: 93
Determinant OurBigBook.com
For a weighted acyclic directed graph, let Mij​ be the sum of path weights from Aj​ to Bi​. Expanding detM gives a signed sum of path families. At the first intersection in a fixed topological order, swap the two path tails. The operation preserves weight and reverses the endpoint permutation's sign, so intersecting families cancel. Only vertex-disjoint families remain. If planarity forces these families to join identically indexed endpoints, their sum has positive sign. Applied to northeast paths with horizontal weight xr​ at height r, this gives the skew Jacobi–Trudi identity.

Determinant of the minimum-index matrix (det(min(i,j))i,j=1n​=1)

Words: 48
Determinant OurBigBook.com
Let L be the triangular matrix with Lij​=1 for j≤i and zero otherwise. Then (LLT)ij​=min(i,j) and detL=1, so the determinant of LLT is one. More generally, for 0=t0​<t1​<⋯<tn​, the matrix with entries min(ti​,tj​) factors as Ldiag(tk​−tk−1​)LT and has determinant ∏k​(tk​−tk−1​). This is the finite-dimensional structure behind the Brownian covariance kernel.

Cauchy–Binet formula

Words: 102
Determinant OurBigBook.com
For matrices A∈Rr×m and B∈Rm×r with r≤m,
det(AB)=∑S⊆{1,…,m}∣S∣=r​​detA:,S​detBS,:​,
(47)
where the indices of S are taken in increasing order. To prove it, write the jth column of AB as ∑q​Bqj​A:,q​ and expand its determinant by multilinearity. Terms with a repeated q vanish by alternation. For each remaining index set S={s1​<⋯<sr​}, collect all permutations qj​=sσ(j)​. The factor from A is sgn(σ)detA:,S​; the sum of the products sgn(σ)∏j​Bsσ(j)​,j​ is detBS,:​. This proves the formula. Applying it to selected rows and columns proves that a product of compatible totally nonnegative matrices is totally nonnegative.

Cramer's rule (xi​=det(Ai​)/det(A))

Words: 59
Determinant OurBigBook.com
For an invertible square matrix A and Ax=b, replace column i by b to form Ai​. Multilinearity of the determinant and b=∑j​xj​A⋅j​ give detAi​=xi​detA: all other summands have repeated columns and vanish. Division gives the formula. With integer coefficients this supplies explicit rational solutions and, together with the Hadamard determinant inequality, bounds their numerators and denominators.

Hadamard determinant inequality (∣detA∣≤∏i​∣ri​∣)

Words: 71
Determinant OurBigBook.com
For a square matrix with row vectors ri​, the absolute determinant is at most the product of the Euclidean norms of its rows. If the rows are dependent the determinant is zero. Otherwise Gram-Schmidt process leaves the determinant unchanged and replaces each row by its component orthogonal to its predecessors. The resulting orthogonal rows have lengths no greater than the original rows, and their volume is their product. This proves the inequality; equality holds for mutually orthogonal rows.

Pfaffian (Pf(A)2=detA)

Words: 54
Determinant OurBigBook.com
For an antisymmetric 2n×2n matrix, the Pfaffian is Pf(A)=(2nn!)−1∑σ∈S2n​​sgn(σ)∏j=1n​Aσ(2j−1),σ(2j)​. Equivalently, it is the coefficient of the top exterior power of the associated alternating form, with the usual factorial normalization. Its square is the determinant. In size four it is a12​a34​−a13​a24​+a14​a23​, so its vanishing characterizes the simple nonzero bivectors of the Klein quadric.

Determinant of a complex block representation (detM=det(A+iB)det(A−iB))

Words: 31
Determinant OurBigBook.com
The block matrix M=(AB​−BA​) is similar over C to diag(A+iB,A−iB) via T=(I−iI​IiI​). Therefore its determinant is det(A+iB)det(A−iB) for arbitrary square matrices A,B. The argument uses a constant change-of-basis matrix and multiplicativity of the determinant.

Words: 35

For a differentiable invertible matrix A(t), dtd​logdetA=tr(A−1A˙) wherever a consistent logarithm is defined. In particular a positive spatial metric tensor satisfies hijh˙ij​=h˙/h. This separates its local volume change from shape change.

Derivative of the determinant (D(det)A​)

Words: 133 Articles: 2
Determinant OurBigBook.com
For an invertible matrix A and any matrix H,
D(det)A​(H)=det(A)tr(A−1H).
(48)
Indeed det(A+tH)=det(A)det(I+tA−1H), and multilinearity shows that the linear coefficient of det(I+tB) is trB. At a singular matrix the derivative is instead written tr(adj(A)H); this polynomial formula holds for all A.

Jacobi's formula (D(det)A​(H)=tr(adj(A)H))

Words: 63
Derivative of the determinant OurBigBook.com
For an arbitrary square matrix A, the derivative of the determinant in direction H is the displayed expression. Differentiating the determinant's multilinear expansion gives the sum of entries of H weighted by their cofactors, equal to the displayed trace. If A is invertible, adj(A)=(detA)A−1 gives (detA)tr(A−1H), and division by detA gives the Jacobi determinant derivative formula for the logarithmic derivative. The adjugate expression remains valid at singular matrices.

Derivative of the determinant OurBigBook.com
The derivative of the determinant at an invertible matrix is DdetA​(K)=detAtr(A−1K). At A=I+H, use det(I+H)=1+trH+O(∥H∥2) and (I+H)−1=I−H+O(∥H∥2). Differentiating the first derivative gives the displayed symmetric bilinear map. More generally D2detA​(H,K)=detA[tr(A−1H)tr(A−1K)−tr(A−1HA−1K)].

Log-determinant (logdetA)

Words: 12
Determinant OurBigBook.com
On positive-definite matrices, the log-determinant has differential dlogdetA=Tr(A−1dA) and is a strictly concave function.

Multilinearity of the determinant

Words: 18
Determinant OurBigBook.com
The determinant is linear in each row and in each column when all the others are held fixed.

Words: 13
Determinant OurBigBook.com
The determinant is multiplicative: for square matrices of the same size, det(AB)=det(A)det(B).

detA=∑σ∈Sn​​sgn(σ)∏i=1n​ai,σ(i)​.

For diagonal entries ai​, superdiagonal entries bi​, and subdiagonal entries ci​, the leading principal determinants satisfy
dn​=an​dn−1​−bn−1​cn−1​dn−2​,d0​=1,d1​=a1​.

Fixed-end spring-chain determinant and its repeated-root limit (DN​=kNUN​((2k−mω2)/(2k)))

Words: 174 Articles: 1
Tridiagonal determinant recurrence OurBigBook.com
For N equal masses joined to fixed walls by equal springs, the stiffness matrix has diagonal 2k and adjacent entries −k. Its characteristic determinant obeys DN​=dDN−1​−k2DN−2​, d=2k−mω2, D0​=1, D1​=d. If β1​+β2​=d and β1​β2​=k2, then DN​=(β1N+1​−β2N+1​)/(β1​−β2​) for distinct roots. At a repeated root β=±k, the correct limit is (N+1)βN, which is nonzero. Thus the apparent ratio solution β1​/β2​=1 must be excluded. Writing d=2kcosq gives DN​=kNsin[(N+1)q]/sinq, the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind. There are exactly N distinct positive normal frequencies 2k/m​sin[jπ/(2(N+1))], 1≤j≤N.
Sine eigenvectors of the fixed-end spring chain
Words: 83
Fixed-end spring-chain determinant and its repeated-root limit OurBigBook.com
For N identical masses between fixed walls with equal springs, the dimensionless stiffness matrix has diagonal entries 2 and adjacent entries −1. Its normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues are
ai(j)​=N+12​​sinN+1ijπ​,λj​=2−2cosN+1jπ​,1≤i,j≤N.
(51)
Extend each vector by a0​=aN+1​=0. The sine addition identity gives 2ai​−ai−1​−ai+1​=λj​ai​, including the fixed-end rows. The finite sine orthogonality identity supplies the normalization and makes distinct vectors orthogonal. The normal mode angular frequencies are ωj​=kλj​/m​ for mass m and spring constant k. This complements the fixed-end spring-chain determinant and its repeated-root limit with the spatial mode shapes.
